cim: Artificial Intelligence In Africa : Majority Of Businesses Adopt AI Technology-Report Shows
cim_eredeti: Artificial Intelligence In Africa : Majority Of Businesses Adopt AI Technology-Report Shows
szoveg_eredeti:
AI is becoming increasingly central to the operating models of surveyed AI businesses.Broader mapping of AI businesses showed that the majority were adopting AI technology into existing services, but a targeted survey showed that 75 percent of respondents consider AI-based products and services as core components of their operating models, according to a report published by GIZ, Germany’s international development agency.

The report notes, this trend is concurrent with the expansion of GenAI tools since 2022, which have broadened access to advanced AI and machine learning capabilities. “These developments highlight the importance of strengthening an enabling environment for inclusive, sustainable, and responsible AI innovation across Africa.”

The AI Made in Africa project by GIZ, explores how African AI businesses are growing, the opportunities they see, and the challenges they face, from the high cost of computing to limited access to specialised talent and the right kind of investment.

GIZ’s AI Made in Africa project aims to help create the conditions for African businesses to develop and benefit from AI. The report presents findings from 311 AI businesses across Africa, alongside 85 African AI businesses that responded to the 2026 African AI Business Survey between April and July 2026, supplemented by interviews with 16 AI businesses, ecosystem support organisations and regulators.

According to the new report, across Africa, businesses are developing artificial intelligence solutions to address challenges in health- care, agriculture, education, finance and other sec- tors. “Their work demonstrates that Africa is not only adopting AI but is increasingly creating technologies shaped by the continent’s needs and realities.”

The study looked at how the African AI business landscape has evolved over the past ten years, combining research on AI businesses across the continent with the first African AI Business Survey. It also included conversations and engagements with AI businesses, policymakers, experts and investors.

The study shows many established start-ups in areas such as agriculture, fintech, healthcare and logistics have adopted AI to improve their existing products and services. But a newer generation of companies, particularly those launched since the rise of generative AI in 2022, are built around AI from the start. For these companies, AI is not an add-on. It is at the heart of what they do.

Developing and selling AI products is expensive

For 65 percent of companies surveyed, cloud computing and AI infrastructure are their biggest costs, often paid in US dollars. At the same time, more than half sell their products for less than US$2,500 per customer a year. This can make it hard to cover the costs of building and running their products. Winning customers’ trust and helping them understand AI are also challenges, cited by 65 percent as barriers to growth.

AI businesses sell to different types of customers. Among those surveyed, 88 percent sell to other businesses, 44 percent serve government customers and 62 percent sell to individual consumers. These figures overlap because a business can serve more than one customer group. Many businesses offer subscriptions, but they also use other ways to make money.

The GIZ study shows companies are investing in their own talent. Finding people with advanced AI skills is difficult, particularly when African companies are competing with employers around the world for experienced professionals. “Many are responding by investing in their existing staff and creating training programmes to help junior employees develop the skills they need.”

According to the report, Businesses need the right kind of investment, not just more investment. African AI companies often face longer sales processes when working with governments and large organisations. “They also have to manage currency risks and the high cost of creating and maintaining their own data. Founders therefore need investors who understand these challenges and are willing to support companies over a longer period, the report notes adding. The issue is not simply a lack of funding, but access to funding that reflects how AI companies in Africa actually grow.

The new report suggests customer trust and AI literacy need to be improved for consumer-level AI adoption.“Companies report spending significant time educating customers, demonstrating AI reliability, and overcoming scepticism around model performance.”

Long procurement processes, legacy systems, and data quality challenges also continue to slow adoption.

Lack of high quality data, was cited among key challenges. One third of surveyed AI businesses pointed out that the lack of data availability, which also leads to high development costs, is one of the leading barriers to scaling.
